Chapter Four: The Cycle of Betrayal and the Struggle to Survive
Over time, a painful pattern started to set in. Promises would be made, treaties signed, and just when it seemed like there might be hope, those agreements were tossed aside or quietly changed whenever it suited the government or new settlers.
And with every new betrayal, fresh hardship followed. It forced families and entire communities to figure out ways to adapt—ways they never would’ve dreamed they’d need.
Picture this—one harsh winter, a group of families waited for food and supplies that had been promised in exchange for their land. But the help never came. Parents could only watch as their children grew thinner and weaker by the day. Some tried to hunt or gather whatever scraps they could, but the land was already stripped bare by soldiers and settlers.
Driven by desperation, a few left the reservation, risking arrest or worse, just to find a meal. Others tried to reason with local officials, but nobody seemed to care. That feeling of betrayal? It was everywhere. How do you trust anyone after that?
And yet, in the middle of all this, people looked out for each other. Neighbors shared whatever little they had. Elders offered comfort and wisdom, while kids learned to make do with almost nothing. Survival became a daily struggle, shaping how everyone saw themselves—and their place in a world that kept turning its back on them.
The toll of all this betrayal was enormous. Some lost hope, turning to alcohol or just giving up. But others leaned into their traditions, finding strength in ceremony and storytelling to keep their spirits alive. The community itself became a lifeline—a source of hope and support when everything else seemed determined to break them.
Most people don’t realize just how much strength it takes to survive when you’re constantly let down. It’s not only about finding food or shelter. It’s about holding onto your dignity—about remembering your worth even when the world keeps sending the opposite message.
Surviving became more than just a necessity. It became a statement—a way to say, “We’re still here. We refuse to be broken.”
And through all the hardship, people kept hoping that things could change, that maybe the next generation would have it better. The cycle of betrayal was hard to break, but the will to survive? That was even stronger.
